chapter.title: Writing a brief the builder can't misread

cards.body: Why is "make it better" the worst thing you can tell a builder? Because they will make it better, by *their* idea of better, and you'll come home to a sauna when you wanted a shelf. **Your message to Claude is the brief you hand the contractor**: the clearer the sheet, the fewer surprises when you walk back in.
cards.simpler: Why is "make it better" the worst thing to tell a builder? They will make it better, but by their own idea of better. You wanted a shelf, and you come home to a sauna. **Your message to Claude is like the instruction sheet you hand a builder.** The clearer the sheet, the fewer surprises when you walk back in.

cards.prompt: You're away for the weekend. The only note on the fridge for your builder says "make the kitchen nicer." What are you most likely to come home to?

options.text: Exactly the spice shelf you had in your head
Something nice, but their idea of nice: gold taps, maybe
An untouched kitchen and a polite note asking what you meant

whyNot.a: That's mind-reading, not a brief: the note never mentioned a shelf, so the builder couldn't know.
whyNot.c: That can happen, but it's not the most likely outcome. The builder has a note to go on, so they'll probably fill the gaps with their own guesses.

cards.reteach: A builder tends to fill gaps in your note with guesses. The fewer details you give, the more guessing they do. Claude often works the same way. Sometimes it asks a question first, but a vague request usually brings back a surprise.

cards.title: Who it's for, and the one job
cards.body:
A brief the builder can't misread answers four questions. Here are the first two.

**Who is it for, and where are they?** "Me, on my phone, standing in a shop" and "my team, on a big office screen" lead to different apps: thumb-sized buttons versus a wide table.

**What is the one job?** Write it as one sentence with one verb: "split a dinner bill," not "help with money stuff." If you need the word *and* twice, you've described two apps. Hire the builder for one.
cards.simpler: A brief the builder can't misread answers four questions. Here are the first two. First, who is it for, and where are they? "Me, on my phone, in a shop" and "my team, on a big office screen" need different apps: big buttons for thumbs, or a wide table. Second, **what is the one job?** Write it as one sentence with one action: "split a dinner bill," not "help with money stuff." If you need "and" twice, that's two apps. Ask for one.

cards.title: Priya's book club
cards.body:
Priya's first message was "make a book club app." Claude came back with sign-up pages, a chat area and a calendar, and none of it did the one thing she needed: pick next month's book. Her second try was five lines:

Build a one-page web app.
For: 6 friends in my book club, on our phones.
Job: vote on next month's book.
Done: 3 titles, a vote button under each, the count beside it.
Leave out: sign-in, comments, a calendar.

She got one page she could test in a minute. **Nobody missed the calendar.**
cards.simpler: Priya first typed "make a book club app." Claude built sign-up pages, a chat area and a calendar, but nothing to pick next month's book, the one thing she needed. Her second try was five lines: a one-page web app, for six friends on their phones, to vote on next month's book, showing 3 titles with a vote button and count by each, with no sign-in, comments or calendar. She could test it in a minute. **Nobody missed the calendar.**

cards.prompt: Sam wants an app for splitting restaurant bills with 3 friends. Which first message is a brief Claude can't misread?

options.text: "Make a really good, modern tip calculator."
"For me and 3 friends, on a phone: type the bill, tap 10, 15 or 20% tip, see what each person pays. No sign-in."
"Make a tip calculator like the best ones out there, but better."

whyNot.a: That's adjectives, not a brief: "good" and "modern" say how you feel, not what to build.
whyNot.c: That's a comparison, not a description: Claude has to guess which "best ones" you mean and what "better" looks like.

cards.reteach: A brief describes things you could point at: a person, a screen, a button, a number. "Good," "modern" and "better" are feelings, and the builder has to guess what they look like. Swap every adjective for something you'd see.

cards.title: What done looks like, and what to leave out
cards.body:
Third question: **what does done look like?** Describe the screen when it works, like taping a photo to the builder's van: "a box for the bill, three tip buttons, each share in big numbers." That's also your checklist for testing it.

Fourth: **what to leave out.** You'd think listing things you *don't* want wastes words. It's the line that does the most work. Claude is an eager builder; ask for a bathroom and you might get heated floors. "No sign-in, no saving, no settings" keeps version one small enough to check in two minutes.
cards.simpler: Third question: **what does done look like?** Picture the working screen, like a photo taped to the builder's van: "a box for the bill, three tip buttons, each share in big numbers." It doubles as your test checklist. Fourth: what to leave out. Oddly, this line does the most work. Claude is eager: ask for a bathroom and you might get heated floors. "No sign-in, no saving, no settings" keeps version one small enough to check in two minutes.

cards.body: Tom's water tracker worked on the first try. Then he typed "make it better." Claude helpfully added dark mode, new fonts and a weekly chart, and moved the +1 button, the only part Tom ever used. **The tell: if your message has nothing you could point at on the screen, it's a wish, not a brief.** "Make the +1 button twice as big" is a brief.
cards.simpler: Tom's water tracker worked the first time. Then he typed "make it better." Claude helpfully added dark mode, new fonts and a weekly chart. It also moved the +1 button, the only part Tom ever used. **If your message names nothing you could point at on the screen, it's a wish, not a brief.** "Make the +1 button twice as big" is a brief.

cards.prompt: Your brief says who it's for, the one job, and what the screen shows when it works. Which part is still missing?

whyNot.a: That's the builder's job, not yours: you describe the house, Claude picks up the hammer.
whyNot.c: That's a detail inside "what done looks like," not its own part, and it can wait for version two.

cards.reteach: Four parts, like four walls: who it's for, the one job, what done looks like, and what to leave out. The last one is the fence. Without it, an eager builder keeps adding rooms.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Before you ask Claude for anything, picture four lines on the fridge note: **who it's for, its one job, what the screen shows when it works, and what to leave out**. Words like "better" make the builder guess; things you can point at make it build.
cards.simpler: Before you ask Claude for anything, picture four lines on the fridge note: **who it's for, its one job, what the screen shows when it works, and what to leave out**. Vague words like "better" make the builder guess. Things you can point at on the screen let it build.

cards.body:
Open Claude Code in an empty folder and type a 5-line brief for something tiny you'd use this week: a packing list, a chore timer. Count your follow-up messages. Two or fewer means the brief did its job.

Next: the files Claude just made, and which one to open first.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in an empty folder. Type a five-line brief for something tiny you'd use this week, like a packing list or a chore timer. Then count how many follow-up messages you need to send. **Two or fewer means the brief did its job.** Next time: the files Claude just made, and which one to open first.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a 5-line brief (who it's for, the one job, what done looks like, what to leave out) that gets a working first version in one or two tries.

dubious_claims: 'a small web app is only 4 kinds of files': it doesn't say which four, and many small web apps are just HTML, CSS and JS (three), so the number looks made up
'This one has a note, so it fills the gaps with its own guesses' (ex. 1, option c): Claude Code often asks a question when a request is vague, so 'it always guesses' is too strong
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' recap has no concrete image, and it holds the chapter's only teaser. That teaser sits one card before the end, so the chapter closes on a try card instead of an open loop.
repairedFrom.fix: Cut the 'Tomorrow' line from card 8. Give card 8 a picture: 'four lines on the fridge note: who, job, done, leave out.' End the try card with a teaser you can check, such as 'Next: the files Claude just made, and which one to open first.'
